<meta>continues from previous page: this section concludes the discussion on Zi Chan, a statesman of the State of Zheng, and begins the commentary on Yan Pingzhong.</meta>

To judge a person by a single word, or to judge an entire era by a single event, is incorrect in both cases. Feng Houzhai said: "If we speak of his involvement in legal reforms and the casting of the bronze penal books <note>The Xing Shu, a legal code cast on bronze tripods in 536 BCE, which was a landmark in Chinese legal history</note>, what he left unfinished was indeed substantial. From the record of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, we know that those who followed the Way of the Gentleman were truly sparse. The words of the Sage neither overflow with excessive praise nor exaggerate faults. The *Collected Commentaries* <term>Jizhu</term> <gloss>The standard Neo-Confucian commentary by Zhu Xi</gloss>, in discussing his righteousness in employing the people, simply follows the reality of his deeds and cannot obscure them."

Mr. Hu said: "The three-year mourning period is the legacy of love <term>yi ai</term> <gloss>the enduring benevolent influence of a ruler</gloss> taught by the disciples of Confucius. The cultivation of the fields and crops, which continued after his death, was the legacy of love taught to our children and younger brothers. The spirit of Zi Chan resides entirely in the concept of Righteousness <term>Yi</term> <gloss>moral duty or justice</gloss>. When the people speak of his kindness <term>Hui</term> but do not understand governance, they are referring only to the single matter of his providing relief to others."

->The Master said: "Yan Pingzhong was skilled in his interactions with others. Even after a long acquaintance, he maintained his respect for them."<-

Yan Pingzhong was a Great Officer of the State of Qi whose given name was Ying. Master Cheng <note>The philosopher Cheng Yi</note> said: "Usually, as a friendship lasts a long time, respect begins to fade. To be able to maintain respect over a long duration..."

<summary>This page concludes a commentary on the statesman Zi Chan's legacy of righteousness and kindness before introducing Confucius's praise for Yan Pingzhong's lasting respect in social relations.</summary>
